
*Notes:* Distributions computed from the 42,835-AI-activity inventory across 543 S&P 500 firms, joined post hoc to the posture-based archetype assignment. "No AI" firms with positive activity counts reflect conference-call statements by firms whose formal SEC filings omit AI entirely. Full 14-variable AI activity profile reported in @tbl-a4-full-archetype-profile (Appendix C).

Vocal Substantives dominate every operational-depth dimension: they report substantially more AI activities, more proprietary technology, more customer-facing deployment, and more production-stage systems. Governance-Led firms occupy an intermediate position, while Defensive Disclosers report the thinnest and least mature operational inventory.

**Controlling for disclosure volume.** Because both semantic frames and AI activities are extracted from the same corporate text, could this activity gap be a trivial artifact of verbosity? To rule out this shared-source confound, we estimate a negative binomial regression of disclosed AI activity counts on disclosure archetypes while explicitly conditioning on total AI disclosure volume ($\log(1 + \text{AI frames})$):

$$
\log \mathbb{E}[\text{AI Activities}_i] = \alpha + \beta_1 \text{VocalSubstantives}_i + \beta_2 \text{GovernanceLed}_i + \gamma \log(1 + \text{Frames}_i)
$$

```{python}
#| label: tbl-4-1b-volume-adjusted
#| tbl-cap: "Disclosed AI activity count by archetype, before and after conditioning on total AI disclosure volume (log frame count). Reference category: Defensive Disclosers."
#| echo: false
import json
from pathlib import Path
from tabulate import tabulate
from IPython.display import Markdown

def _p(name):
    p = Path(f"../data/processed/clusters/{name}")
    return p if p.exists() else Path(f"data/processed/clusters/{name}")

reg = json.loads(_p("strategy_dimensions_manifest.json").read_text())["activity_volume_regression"]
OTHERS = ["Governance-Led Disclosers", "Vocal Substantives"]

def fmt_p(p):
    return "<0.001" if p < 0.001 else f"{p:.3f}"

rows = [[a, f"{reg['raw'][a]['ratio']:.2f}x", fmt_p(reg['raw'][a]['p']),
        f"{reg['volume_adjusted'][a]['ratio']:.2f}x", fmt_p(reg['volume_adjusted'][a]['p'])] for a in OTHERS]
rows.append(["log(1 + AI frames)", "-", "-", f"{reg['log_frames_coef']:+.2f} (coef.)", fmt_p(reg['log_frames_p'])])
Markdown(tabulate(rows, headers=[f"Archetype vs. {reg['reference']}", "Raw ratio", "p", "Volume-adjusted ratio", "p"]))
```

Total AI disclosure volume explains most of the raw gap (log frame count alone reaches $R^2 = 0.74$ in the adjusted model), exactly as the shared-source-text concern predicts. But a real difference survives conditioning on it: at the same total disclosure volume, Vocal Substantives still report **2.33 times as many AI activities** as Defensive Disclosers ($p < 0.001$) and Governance-Led Disclosers report **1.38 times as many** ($p < 0.001$). Communication posture is not merely verbosity; it reflects different intensities of disclosed operational AI activity.

## What are firms actually doing differently?

The operational distinction between archetypes extends beyond AI activity counts to the substantive business purpose of their AI initiatives (@fig-archetype-activity-mix):

```{python}
#| label: fig-archetype-activity-mix
#| fig-cap: "Mix of disclosed corporate AI activities by disclosure archetype (100% stacked horizontal bars). Vocal Substantives dedicate over 60% of AI activities to client products (Sell); Governance-Led prioritize internal operations (Operate) and governance control (Control)."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9.2
#| fig-height: 3.6
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def _p(name):
    p = Path(f"../data/processed/clusters/{name}")
    return p if p.exists() else Path(f"data/processed/clusters/{name}")

df_strat = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_strategy_dimensions.parquet"))
act = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_activities.parquet")).merge(df_strat[["ticker", "archetype"]], on="ticker", how="left")
act["archetype"] = act["archetype"].fillna("No AI")

def get_role(row):
    f = str(row["function_family"])
    obj = str(row["object_family"])
    tgt = str(row["target"])
    if f in ["product_feature", "content_and_media"] or "product" in obj or tgt == "customers":
        return "Sell (Customer products)"
    elif f in ["customer_service", "marketing_and_sales"]:
        return "Serve (Sales & service)"
    elif f in ["software_development", "hr_and_talent"] or "copilot" in obj or "talent" in obj:
        return "Enable (Productivity & dev)"
    elif f in ["it_and_cybersecurity", "fraud_and_risk", "governance"] or "security" in obj or "governance" in obj:
        return "Control (Risk & security)"
    elif f in ["ai_compute_and_models", "research_and_product_development", "data_and_analytics"] or "compute" in obj or "analytics" in obj:
        return "Build (Compute & data)"
    else:
        return "Operate (Internal operations)"

act["role"] = act.apply(get_role, axis=1)
ARCH = ["Vocal Substantives", "Governance-Led Disclosers", "Defensive Disclosers"]
ct_mix = pd.crosstab(act["archetype"], act["role"], normalize="index") * 100

roles_order = [
    "Sell (Customer products)",
    "Operate (Internal operations)",
    "Build (Compute & data)",
    "Enable (Productivity & dev)",
    "Control (Risk & security)",
    "Serve (Sales & service)"
]
colors = ["#1D4ED8", "#0D9488", "#D97706", "#6366F1", "#DC2626", "#E11D48"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.2, 3.6), dpi=300)
y_pos = np.arange(3)
left = np.zeros(3)

for role, col in zip(roles_order, colors):
    vals = [ct_mix.loc[a, role] for a in ARCH]
    bars = ax.barh(y_pos, vals, left=left, color=col, edgecolor="white", height=0.55, label=role)
    for idx, (b, v) in enumerate(zip(bars, vals)):
        if v >= 6.0:
            ax.text(left[idx] + v/2, b.get_y() + b.get_height()/2, f"{v:.1f}%",
                    ha="center", va="center", color="white", fontsize=7.8, fontweight="bold")
    left += vals

ax.set_yticks(y_pos)
ax.set_yticklabels(ARCH, fontsize=9.0, fontweight="bold")
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_xlim(0, 100)
ax.set_xlabel("% of Disclosed AI Activities", fontsize=8.8, fontweight="bold")
ax.set_title("Mix of Disclosed Corporate AI Activities by Disclosure Archetype (100% Stacked)",
             fontsize=10.0, fontweight="bold", pad=12)
ax.legend(bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.22), loc="upper center", ncol=3, fontsize=8.0, frameon=False)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The 100% stacked distribution in @fig-archetype-activity-mix reveals stark strategic divergences in where AI enters the firm:

1. **Vocal Substantives focus on revenue-generating products:** Nearly two-thirds of their disclosed AI activities (**61.8%**) belong to **Sell** (embedding AI directly into customer products and services), while internal operations account for only 19.5%.
2. **Governance-Led Disclosers emphasize operational efficiency and control:** Their AI activity mix is led by **Operate** (39.7%) and **Sell** (38.1%), but they devote the highest share among all groups to **Control** (4.5% in risk, fraud detection, and model governance).
3. **Defensive Disclosers mirror back-office automation:** Their AI activities split between **Sell** (43.0%) and **Operate** (37.6%), with heightened focus on **Serve** (2.9% in customer service bots), reflecting utility and efficiency use cases rather than technological leadership.

## Decomposing AI Activity Grounding

While firms disclose thousands of AI activities, a critical empirical question is how concretely and specifically these AI activities are grounded in corporate text. To evaluate AI activity grounding ($G$), we decompose all 42,835 disclosed AI activities across escalating verification requirements:

$$\text{AI Activity Claim} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{Specific Business Function} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{Deployed Stage} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{Named Product/Process} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{Quantified Outcome Metric}$$

```{python}
#| label: fig-ladder-substance
#| fig-cap: "Decomposing AI activity grounding: cumulative nested progression of evidence requirements (left) and independent grounding attribute frequencies (right) across all disclosed AI activities."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9.6
#| fig-height: 3.8
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

data_path = Path("../data/processed/clusters/firm_activities.parquet")
if not data_path.exists():
    data_path = Path("data/processed/clusters/firm_activities.parquet")

df = pd.read_parquet(data_path)
n_total = len(df)

# Nested counts
c1 = n_total
c2 = len(df[df["function_family"] != "unspecified"])
c3 = len(df[(df["function_family"] != "unspecified") & df["stage"].isin(["deployed", "scaled"])])
c4 = len(df[(df["function_family"] != "unspecified") & df["stage"].isin(["deployed", "scaled"]) & df["evidence_strength"].isin(["named_product_or_process", "metric"])])
c5 = len(df[(df["function_family"] != "unspecified") & df["stage"].isin(["deployed", "scaled"]) & (df["evidence_strength"] == "metric")])

pcts_nested = [c / n_total * 100 for c in [c1, c2, c3, c4, c5]]

# Independent component rates
p_func = (df["function_family"] != "unspecified").mean() * 100
p_stage = df["stage"].isin(["deployed", "scaled"]).mean() * 100
p_named = df["evidence_strength"].isin(["named_product_or_process", "metric"]).mean() * 100
p_metric = (df["evidence_strength"] == "metric").mean() * 100
p_vendor = (df["ai_source"] == "third_party").mean() * 100

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 3.8), dpi=300)

labels_nested = [
    "1. Discloses an AI activity claim",
    "2. + Specific business function",
    "3. + Deployed / scaled stage",
    "4. + Named product or process",
    "5. + Quantified outcome / metric"
]
colors_nested = ["#94A3B8", "#64748B", "#3B82F6", "#2563EB", "#1D4ED8"]
bars1 = ax1.barh(labels_nested[::-1], pcts_nested[::-1], color=colors_nested[::-1], height=0.6)
for b, p in zip(bars1, pcts_nested[::-1]):
    ax1.text(p + 1.5, b.get_y() + b.get_height() / 2, f"{p:.1f}%", va="center", fontsize=8.5, fontweight="bold", color="#1E293B")
ax1.set_xlim(0, 115)
ax1.set_xlabel(f"% of all {n_total:,} disclosed AI activities", fontsize=8.8, fontweight="bold")
ax1.set_title("Decomposing AI Activity Grounding\n(Strictly Nested Concreteness Requirements)", fontsize=9.8, fontweight="bold")
ax1.grid(True, axis="x", linestyle="--", alpha=0.3)
ax1.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

labels_ind = [
    "Deployed or scaled stage",
    "Specific business function",
    "Named product or process",
    "Quantified outcome metric",
    "External vendor / model attributed"
]
pcts_ind = [p_stage, p_func, p_named, p_metric, p_vendor]
colors_ind = ["#059669", "#0284C7", "#6366F1", "#D97706", "#DC2626"]
bars2 = ax2.barh(labels_ind[::-1], pcts_ind[::-1], color=colors_ind[::-1], height=0.6)
for b, p in zip(bars2, pcts_ind[::-1]):
    ax2.text(p + 1.5, b.get_y() + b.get_height() / 2, f"{p:.1f}%", va="center", fontsize=8.5, fontweight="bold", color="#1E293B")
ax2.set_xlim(0, 115)
ax2.set_xlabel("% of AI activities with attribute present", fontsize=8.8, fontweight="bold")
ax2.set_title("Independent AI Grounding Attributes\n(% of AI activities meeting each criterion)", fontsize=9.8, fontweight="bold")
ax2.grid(True, axis="x", linestyle="--", alpha=0.3)
ax2.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

As shown in @fig-ladder-substance, while 68.0% of AI activities specify a business function and 51.1% are deployed in production, the share that names a tangible product or process drops to 28.3%. Furthermore, only 7.7% of all disclosed AI activities satisfy the full nested progression by coupling an operational deployment to a quantified performance metric. Most disclosed AI activities remain difficult to externally evaluate because they are not accompanied by quantified outcomes.

## The paradox of the GenAI boom

Tracking these grounding dimensions over time reveals a central empirical paradox: **did the post-2023 generative AI boom produce more grounded corporate disclosure?**

The evidence indicates the exact opposite: **disclosed AI activity volume surged, but marginal concreteness deteriorated** (@fig-volume-vs-grounding).

```{python}
#| label: fig-volume-vs-grounding
#| fig-cap: "The paradox of the GenAI boom: disclosed AI activity volume surged 4.9-fold (Panel A), while marginal concreteness and grounding indicators deteriorated (Panel B), 2021–2025 (2026 shown as year-to-date)."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9.8
#| fig-height: 4.0
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
import duckdb
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

db_path = Path("../duckdb/thesis.duckdb")
if not db_path.exists():
    db_path = Path("duckdb/thesis.duckdb")
act_path = Path("../data/processed/clusters/firm_activities.parquet")
if not act_path.exists():
    act_path = Path("data/processed/clusters/firm_activities.parquet")

act = pd.read_parquet(act_path)
con = duckdb.connect(str(db_path), read_only=True)
filings = con.execute("""
    WITH manifest AS (
        SELECT country_code, accession_number, filing_date FROM filing_manifest WHERE form_type != 'Earnings call transcript'
        UNION ALL
        SELECT country_code, accession_number, filing_date FROM filing_manifest_10q
    )
    SELECT accession_number, filing_date FROM manifest
""").df()
con.close()

act_f = act[act.channel == "filing"].merge(filings, on="accession_number", how="left")
act_f["year"] = pd.to_datetime(act_f["filing_date"]).dt.year
act_c = act[act.channel == "call"].copy()
act_c["year"] = act_c["accession_number"].str.extract(r"_(\d{4})Q")[0].astype(float)
both = pd.concat([act_f, act_c], ignore_index=True)
both = both[both["year"].between(2021, 2026)]
both["year"] = both["year"].astype(int)

vol = both.groupby("year").size()
dep_share = both.groupby("year")["stage"].apply(lambda s: (s == "deployed").mean() * 100)
gen_ev = both.groupby("year")["evidence_strength"].apply(lambda s: (s == "generic").mean() * 100)
named_prod = both.groupby("year")["evidence_strength"].apply(lambda s: (s == "named_product_or_process").mean() * 100)
ident_func = both.groupby("year")["function_family"].apply(lambda s: (s != "unspecified").mean() * 100)

# Dynamic projection for 2026 based on observed elapsed filing months
latest_date_2026 = act_f[act_f["year"] == 2026]["filing_date"].max()
months_observed = latest_date_2026.month if pd.notnull(latest_date_2026) else 8
annual_factor = 12.0 / months_observed
vol_2026_obs = vol[2026]
vol_2026_proj_total = int(round(vol_2026_obs * annual_factor))
vol_2026_proj_adj = vol_2026_proj_total - vol_2026_obs

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.0, 4.2), dpi=300)

years = sorted(vol.index.tolist())
main_years = [y for y in years if y <= 2025]
ytd_years = [y for y in years if y >= 2025]

# Panel A: Total Disclosed Corporate AI Activities with Stacked Year-End Projection
bars_hist = ax1.bar(main_years, [vol[y] for y in main_years], color="#2563EB", width=0.55, edgecolor="#1D4ED8", lw=1.2, label="Observed full-year AI activities")
bar_26_obs = ax1.bar([2026], [vol_2026_obs], color="#60A5FA", width=0.55, edgecolor="#2563EB", lw=1.2, label="2026 YTD observed AI activities")
bar_26_proj = ax1.bar([2026], [vol_2026_proj_adj], bottom=[vol_2026_obs], color="#DBEAFE", width=0.55,
                      edgecolor="#1D4ED8", lw=1.2, linestyle="--", hatch="///", label="Projected year-end AI activity adjustment")

max_v = max(max(vol[y] for y in main_years), vol_2026_proj_total)
ax1.set_ylim(0, max_v * 1.20)

for y in main_years:
    v = vol[y]
    ax1.text(y, v + max_v * 0.02, f"{v:,}", ha="center", fontsize=8.2, fontweight="bold", color="#1E293B")

ax1.text(2026, vol_2026_obs * 0.55, f"{vol_2026_obs:,}\n(YTD)", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.8, fontweight="bold", color="#1E3A8A")
ax1.text(2026, vol_2026_proj_total + max_v * 0.02, f"{vol_2026_proj_total:,}\n(FY Proj.)", ha="center", fontsize=8.0, fontweight="bold", color="#1D4ED8")

ax1.set_ylabel("Number of Disclosed AI Activities", fontsize=9.0, fontweight="bold")
ax1.set_xlabel("Year", fontsize=9.0, fontweight="bold")
ax1.set_xticks(years)
ax1.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=7.2, framealpha=0.9)
growth_ratio = vol[2025] / vol[2021]
proj_ratio = vol_2026_proj_total / vol[2021]
ax1.set_title(f"Panel A: AI Activity Volume Surges ({growth_ratio:.1f}× panel, {proj_ratio:.1f}× proj.)\nTotal Disclosed Corporate AI Activities", fontsize=9.5, fontweight="bold")
ax1.grid(True, axis="y", linestyle="--", alpha=0.3)
ax1.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

# Panel B: Marginal Concreteness Weakens
def _trend_label(base, series):
    return f"{base} ({series[main_years[0]]:.0f}% → {series[main_years[-1]]:.0f}%)"

ax2.plot(main_years, [dep_share[y] for y in main_years], "o-", color="#059669", lw=2.2, ms=5, label=_trend_label("Deployed in production", dep_share))
ax2.plot(ytd_years, [dep_share[y] for y in ytd_years], "o:", color="#059669", lw=1.8, ms=5)
ax2.plot(main_years, [ident_func[y] for y in main_years], "s-", color="#0284C7", lw=2.2, ms=5, label=_trend_label("Identifiable business function", ident_func))
ax2.plot(ytd_years, [ident_func[y] for y in ytd_years], "s:", color="#0284C7", lw=1.8, ms=5)
ax2.plot(main_years, [named_prod[y] for y in main_years], "^-", color="#6366F1", lw=2.2, ms=5, label=_trend_label("Named product or process", named_prod))
ax2.plot(ytd_years, [named_prod[y] for y in ytd_years], "^:", color="#6366F1", lw=1.8, ms=5)
ax2.plot(main_years, [gen_ev[y] for y in main_years], "d--", color="#DC2626", lw=2.2, ms=5, label=_trend_label("Generic, unanchored evidence", gen_ev))
ax2.plot(ytd_years, [gen_ev[y] for y in ytd_years], "d:", color="#DC2626", lw=1.8, ms=5)

all_shares = pd.concat([dep_share, ident_func, named_prod, gen_ev])
min_s, max_s = all_shares.min(), all_shares.max()
s_range = max_s - min_s
ax2.set_ylim(max(0, min_s - s_range * 0.15), min(100, max_s + s_range * 0.40))
ax2.set_ylabel("Share of Disclosed AI Activities (%)", fontsize=9.0, fontweight="bold")
ax2.set_xlabel("Year", fontsize=9.0, fontweight="bold")
ax2.set_xticks(years)
ax2.legend(fontsize=7.2, loc="upper right", framealpha=0.92)
ax2.set_title("Panel B: Marginal Concreteness Weakens\nGrounding and Specificity Indicators Over Time", fontsize=9.5, fontweight="bold")
ax2.grid(True, linestyle="--", alpha=0.3)
ax2.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

fig.suptitle("The Paradox of the GenAI Boom: Disclosed AI Activity Expanded Faster than Observable Grounding",
             fontsize=10.5, fontweight="bold", y=0.98)
plt.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0, 1, 0.94])
plt.show()
```

Crucially, this finding does not claim that real-world firm capabilities deteriorated. Rather, it establishes an informational phenomenon: **the marginal corporate AI activity disclosed following ChatGPT was less concrete, less mature, and more speculative than the disclosures preceding it**.

## Who owns the AI?

A fundamental question for investors and regulators evaluating corporate AI claims is technological provenance: are public firms genuine technology creators, or commercial consumers of foundation models developed by third-party hyperscalers?

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

def _p(name):
    p = Path(f"../data/processed/clusters/{name}")
    return p if p.exists() else Path(f"data/processed/clusters/{name}")

df = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_activities.parquet"))
n_activities_total = len(df)

def check_role(entities, roles):
    if entities is None or len(entities) == 0:
        return False
    return any(e.get("role") in roles for e in entities)

own_brand_pct = df["named_entities"].apply(lambda l: check_role(l, ["own_product_or_brand"])).mean() * 100
ext_vendor_pct = df["named_entities"].apply(lambda l: check_role(l, ["external_provider", "external_model"])).mean() * 100
partner_pct = df["named_entities"].apply(lambda l: check_role(l, ["partner"])).mean() * 100
third_party_src = (df["ai_source"] == "third_party").mean() * 100
any_ext_provider = df.groupby("ticker")["named_entities"].apply(lambda s: s.apply(lambda l: check_role(l, ["external_provider", "external_model", "partner"])).any())
ext_provider_firm_pct = 100 * any_ext_provider.mean()

_VENDOR_PATTERNS = {
    "OpenAI / Microsoft Ecosystem": r"openai|chatgpt|gpt|copilot|microsoft|azure",
    "Alphabet / Google": r"google|gemini|vertex|bard|deepmind|palm",
    "NVIDIA": r"nvidia|cuda",
    "Amazon Web Services": r"amazon|aws|bedrock|sagemaker",
}

def _vendor_firm_pct(pattern):
    import re
    def has_vendor(entities):
        if entities is None or len(entities) == 0:
            return False
        return any(e.get("role") in ("external_provider", "external_model", "partner") and re.search(pattern, str(e.get("name", "")).lower()) for e in entities)
    by_firm = df.groupby("ticker")["named_entities"].apply(lambda s: s.apply(has_vendor).any())
    return 100 * by_firm.mean()

vendor_pcts = {name: _vendor_firm_pct(pat) for name, pat in _VENDOR_PATTERNS.items()}
```

Comparing named entity roles across the `{python} f"{n_activities_total:,}"` disclosed AI activity statements exposes a marked provenance asymmetry (@fig-tech-provenance):

- **`{python} f"{own_brand_pct:.1f}"`%** of all disclosed AI activity statements explicitly attach a proprietary corporate brand or in-house product name to the AI deployment.
- **`{python} f"{ext_vendor_pct:.1f}"`%** explicitly cite an external technology vendor or foundation model (and `{python} f"{partner_pct:.1f}"`% name a commercial partner).
- This occurs despite **`{python} f"{ext_provider_firm_pct:.1f}"`%** of all S&P 500 firms disclosing at least one external technology provider, model family, or hyperscaler somewhere within their broader disclosures.

```{python}
#| label: fig-tech-provenance
#| fig-cap: "Technology provenance: proprietary branding vs. external vendor attribution across corporate AI activities."
#| echo: false

#| fig-height: 3.2
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

categories = [
    "Proprietary corporate brand or product named",
    "Third-party external source declared (ai_source)",
    "External foundation model or vendor named",
    "Commercial strategic partner named"
]
values = [own_brand_pct, third_party_src, ext_vendor_pct, partner_pct]
colors = ["#1D4ED8", "#64748B", "#DC2626", "#EA580C"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.8, 3.2), dpi=300)
bars = ax.barh(categories[::-1], values[::-1], color=colors[::-1], height=0.55)

for b, v in zip(bars, values[::-1]):
    ax.text(v + 0.8, b.get_y() + b.get_height() / 2, f"{v:.1f}%", va="center", fontsize=8.8, fontweight="bold", color="#0F172A")

ax.set_xlim(0, 45)
ax.set_xlabel(f"% of all disclosed AI activity statements (n = {n_activities_total:,})", fontsize=9.0, fontweight="bold")

             fontsize=10.2, fontweight="bold")
```

When external vendors are identified, the ecosystem is highly concentrated around four hyperscalers: OpenAI / Microsoft Ecosystem (cited by `{python} f"{vendor_pcts['OpenAI / Microsoft Ecosystem']:.1f}"`% of firms), Alphabet / Google (`{python} f"{vendor_pcts['Alphabet / Google']:.1f}"`%), NVIDIA (`{python} f"{vendor_pcts['NVIDIA']:.1f}"`%), and Amazon Web Services (`{python} f"{vendor_pcts['Amazon Web Services']:.1f}"`%). The complete vendor taxonomy (@tbl-vendor-ecosystem) and named entity distribution (@tbl-entity-roles) are reported in Appendix C.

Corporate disclosures disproportionately foreground proprietary brands while identifying the external technology stack far less frequently.

### Regional Orientation of AI Disclosure

Beyond the broad divide between proprietary branding and external attribution, a related strategic dimension concerns the **regional orientation of AI disclosure**: when S&P 500 corporations discuss artificial intelligence, which geographic ecosystems -- named technology providers, but also markets, competitors, and regulatory regimes -- do they orient that discussion around?

We measure this with a lexical taxonomy applied strictly within AI-context text: paragraphs that already carry an extracted AI disclosure frame. A mention is any word-boundary match, inside such a paragraph, of a term mapped to a region in the taxonomy -- named technology entities (foundation models, hyperscalers, chipmakers, enterprise platforms) together with literal country and demonym terms (e.g. "China," "Chinese," "Japan"). Because the scan is confined to paragraphs already tied to AI content, a mention never comes from an unrelated supply-chain or tariff risk-factor paragraph that happens to name a country. Regions are United States, Europe, China, and Other (the complete term list is documented in Appendix C). United States is measured asymmetrically: it is matched only by named technology entities (e.g. "OpenAI," "NVIDIA"), never by the literal country name, because every U.S.-domiciled filer routinely names its own jurisdiction and a literal match there would trivially saturate the United States share; every other region is matched by both named entities and literal country/demonym terms. This means the United States share below is, if anything, understated relative to the other three regions' measurement.

Two empirical patterns stand out (@fig-geo-provenance):

1. **U.S. Ecosystem Concentration, Understated by Construction:** References to the United States dominate AI-context disclosure, accounting for **`{python} f"{geo_us_share:.1f}"`%** of all regionally classified mentions (`{python} f"{geo_us_n:.0f}"` of `{python} f"{geo_total_mentions:,}"` mentions across `{python} geo_us_firms` firms), against Europe (`{python} f"{geo_eu_share:.1f}"`%) and the aggregate Other bloc (`{python} f"{geo_other_share:.1f}"`%). Because United States mentions are counted only through named technology entities while every other region additionally benefits from literal country/demonym matches, this gap holds despite -- not because of -- how the measure is built.
2. **Chinese References Are a Stable, Low-Double-Digit Minority:** Chinese references hold between **`{python} f"{geo_cn_min_share:.1f}"`%** (`{python} geo_cn_min_year`) and **`{python} f"{geo_cn_max_share:.1f}"`%** (`{python} geo_cn_max_year`) of regionally classified mentions across the sample, including a rise to `{python} f"{geo_cn_2025_share:.1f}"`% (`{python} geo_cn_2025_n` mentions) in 2025 that coincides with the release of DeepSeek's open-weight reasoning models, before settling back to `{python} f"{geo_cn_2026_share:.1f}"`% (`{python} geo_cn_2026_n` mentions) in the 2026 year-to-date sample -- within the range observed since 2021, not a decline.

AI disclosure remains oriented overwhelmingly around U.S. technology and market context, even under a measurement asymmetry that structurally favors every other region.

## External Characterization of Archetypes: Fundamental Financial Profiles

Unlike the activity inventory extracted from disclosure text, financial fundamentals and market prices come from independent XBRL filings and market returns. We test whether the empirical archetypes correspond to economically distinct firms, both unconditionally and after sector-by-year adjustment ($X = \alpha_{s,y} + \gamma \cdot \text{Archetype} + \varepsilon$, referenced against No AI, with firm-clustered standard errors).

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import json
from pathlib import Path

def _p(name):
    p = Path(f"../data/processed/clusters/{name}")
    return p if p.exists() else Path(f"data/processed/clusters/{name}")

_econ = json.loads(_p("strategy_economic_profiles.json").read_text())
econ_a = _econ["panel_a"]
d = _econ["panel_b"]

def _pfmt(p):
    return "< 0.001" if p < 0.001 else f"= {p:.3g}"

def _reg(key, seg):
    row = d[key][seg]
    return row["gamma"], row["se"], row["p"]

vs_mktcap_g, _, vs_mktcap_p = _reg("log_market_cap", "Vocal Substantives")
vs_rd_g, _, vs_rd_p = _reg("rd_intensity", "Vocal Substantives")
vs_gm_g, _, vs_gm_p = _reg("gross_margin", "Vocal Substantives")
vs_beta_g, _, vs_beta_p = _reg("beta", "Vocal Substantives")
vs_ps_g, _, vs_ps_p = _reg("ps_ratio", "Vocal Substantives")

gov_mktcap_g, _, gov_mktcap_p = _reg("log_market_cap", "Governance-Led Disclosers")
gov_roic_g, _, gov_roic_p = _reg("roic_minus_wacc", "Governance-Led Disclosers")
gov_ps_g, _, gov_ps_p = _reg("ps_ratio", "Governance-Led Disclosers")

def_rd_g, _, def_rd_p = _reg("rd_intensity", "Defensive Disclosers")

rd_vs, rd_gov, rd_def = econ_a["Vocal Substantives"]["rd_intensity"], econ_a["Governance-Led Disclosers"]["rd_intensity"], econ_a["Defensive Disclosers"]["rd_intensity"]
gm_vs, gm_gov, gm_def = econ_a["Vocal Substantives"]["gross_margin"], econ_a["Governance-Led Disclosers"]["gross_margin"], econ_a["Defensive Disclosers"]["gross_margin"]
beta_vs, beta_gov, beta_def = econ_a["Vocal Substantives"]["beta"], econ_a["Governance-Led Disclosers"]["beta"], econ_a["Defensive Disclosers"]["beta"]
```

Crude medians already put Vocal Substantives ahead of the other two archetypes on the dimensions that matter most for a technology-intensive segment: R&D/sales `{python} f"{100*rd_vs:.1f}"`% vs. `{python} f"{100*min(rd_gov, rd_def):.1f}"`–`{python} f"{100*max(rd_gov, rd_def):.1f}"`% for the other archetypes, gross margin `{python} f"{100*gm_vs:.1f}"`% vs. `{python} f"{100*min(gm_gov, gm_def):.1f}"`–`{python} f"{100*max(gm_gov, gm_def):.1f}"`%, beta `{python} f"{beta_vs:.2f}"` vs. `{python} f"{min(beta_gov, beta_def):.2f}"`–`{python} f"{max(beta_gov, beta_def):.2f}"`. The residualized panel, within the same sector and year, confirms each archetype separately:

- **Vocal Substantives** is the most consistently distinct archetype: `{python} f"{vs_mktcap_g:+.2f}"` log points of market cap ($p$ `{python} _pfmt(vs_mktcap_p)`), `{python} f"{100*vs_rd_g:+.1f}"` percentage points of R&D-to-sales ($p$ `{python} _pfmt(vs_rd_p)`), `{python} f"{100*vs_gm_g:+.1f}"` points of gross margin ($p$ `{python} _pfmt(vs_gm_p)`), `{python} f"{vs_beta_g:+.2f}"` of beta ($p$ `{python} _pfmt(vs_beta_p)`), and `{python} f"{vs_ps_g:+.2f}"` of price-to-sales ($p$ `{python} _pfmt(vs_ps_p)`).
- **Governance-Led Disclosers** separate from No AI mainly on scale and earnings quality rather than technology intensity: a market-cap premium (`{python} f"{gov_mktcap_g:+.2f}"` log points, $p$ `{python} _pfmt(gov_mktcap_p)`) and a ROIC-minus-WACC premium (`{python} f"{gov_roic_g:+.3f}"`, $p$ `{python} _pfmt(gov_roic_p)`), but a price-to-sales effect of `{python} f"{gov_ps_g:+.2f}"` ($p$ `{python} _pfmt(gov_ps_p)`). This is consistent with the archetype being defined by governance-heavy disclosure that correlates with firm size and regulatory exposure (larger, more heavily regulated firms disclose more governance content) rather than with distinctive AI economics.
- **Defensive Disclosers** separate least from No AI: an R&D effect of `{python} f"{100*def_rd_g:+.1f}"` points ($p$ `{python} _pfmt(def_rd_p)`) is the most notable dimension.

The story that survives sector-year adjustment is that the archetype most concretely grounded in disclosed AI activity (Vocal Substantives, @tbl-4-1-archetype-profile) is also the one most consistently distinct on firm fundamentals, not that talking about AI, or emphasizing governance, is by itself.

# Credibility Under Increasing Disclosure Commitment

In the absence of an audited census of corporate artificial intelligence deployment, what observable evidence makes a corporate AI claim credible? Rather than treating credibility as an unobservable moral state, this chapter tests how disclosures behave across escalating verification costs and reporting commitments (@fig-credibility-ladder): within-filing substantiation, cross-venue persistence from oral calls to statutory filings, and responsive adjustment under direct SEC scrutiny.

## Empirical Credibility Tests: The Credibility Ladder

Credibility is revealed not by unvarnished claims of internal capability, but by what survives as disclosure becomes progressively more costly to commit to.

## Where Disclosure Runs Ahead of Substance

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import json
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

def _p(name):
    p = Path(f"../data/processed/clusters/{name}")
    return p if p.exists() else Path(f"data/processed/clusters/{name}")

_df_w = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_year_washing_score.parquet"))
_w = _df_w["w"].dropna()
_validation = json.loads(_p("washing_score_validation.json").read_text())
n_firm_years = _validation["n_panel"]
n_firms_panel = _validation["n_firms"]
year_min, year_max = int(_df_w["year"].min()), int(_df_w["year"].max())
```

Using the measurement constructs defined in Chapter 2, we evaluate whether a firm's disclosure volume scales with its concrete operational substance across `{python} f"{n_firm_years:,}"` disclosing firm-years (`{python} n_firms_panel` S&P 500 firms, `{python} year_min`–`{python} year_max`, `{python} year_max` shown as year-to-date). The **decoupling index ($W_{it}$)** measures the signed difference between the percentile ranks of AI Disclosure Intensity ($D_{it}$) and Disclosed Substance ($S_{it}$):
$$
W_{it} = \text{pct\_rank}(D_{it}) - \text{pct\_rank}(S_{it}) \in [-1, 1]
$$
By construction, $W = 0$ reflects commensurate communication, $W > 0$ indicates narrative running ahead of verifiable substance ("decoupling"), and $W < 0$ captures "quiet substance."

```{python}
#| label: fig-washing-distribution
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of corporate AI disclosure–substance decoupling (W). Values of W > 0 represent narrative intensity running ahead of disclosed substance; values of W < 0 denote quiet substance. The top 5% decoupled tail is highlighted in red."

#| fig-height: 4.0
```

## What Changes from Filing to Call?

If decoupling constitutes an enduring communication posture, what happens when the same firm discusses AI across disclosure venues with contrasting legal liabilities?

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import json
from pathlib import Path

def _p(name):
    p = Path(f"../data/processed/clusters/{name}")
    return p if p.exists() else Path(f"data/processed/clusters/{name}")

grounding = json.loads(_p("activity_grounding.json").read_text())
gap = grounding["channel_gap"]
gap_n_cells, gap_n_firms = gap["n_cells"], gap["n_firms"]
```

We evaluate this using a **Firm × Fiscal-Year fixed effects design** ($\alpha_{i,t}$) across `{python} gap_n_cells` balanced firm-year cells (`{python} gap_n_firms` firms) with $\ge 3$ disclosed AI activities in both channels:

$$
Y_{i,t,\text{venue}} = \alpha_{i,t} + \beta \, \mathbf{1}[\text{venue} = \text{Call}] + \varepsilon_{i,t,\text{venue}}
$$

Because each cell contains exactly two observations—the firm's voluntary earnings call and its mandatory statutory SEC filing (10-K/10-Q) for the exact same fiscal year—the estimator measures the within-firm, within-period venue-associated difference ($\text{Call}_{i,t} - \text{Filing}_{i,t}$). This sweeps out all time-invariant firm unobservables, business models, and macroeconomic conditions.

The results reveal a stark contrast between what firms claim to do and the evidence they attach to those claims (@fig-venue-call-filing-differences).

```{python}
#| label: fig-venue-call-filing-differences
#| fig-cap: "Call-minus-filing differences in AI activity composition and evidentiary grounding within the same firm and fiscal year (95% confidence intervals). Panel A demonstrates that core AI activity shares are preserved across venues. Panel B shows that statutory filings contain substantially fewer verifiable operational details."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8.0
#| fig-height: 5.0
import json
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

def _p(name):
    p = Path(f"../data/processed/clusters/{name}")
    return p if p.exists() else Path(f"data/processed/clusters/{name}")

_pooled = json.loads(_p("activity_grounding.json").read_text())["channel_gap"]["pooled"]

def _gap_ci(family):
    row = _pooled[family]
    gap, t, p = row["gap_pp"], row["t"], row["p"]
    se = abs(gap / t) if t else 0.0
    return gap, gap - 1.96 * se, gap + 1.96 * se, p

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8.0, 5.0), dpi=300, sharex=True,
                               gridspec_kw={'height_ratios': [1, 1.8]})

FAMILIES1 = ["proprietary_ai", "internal_deployment", "customer_facing_deployment"]
labels1 = [
    'Proprietary AI development',
    'Internal operational deployment',
    'Customer-facing deployment',
```

## Promotion is Not the Opposite of Evidence

A common assumption in corporate communication research is that promotional tone is inversely related to credibility: that high promotion reflects empty hype, whereas low promotion signifies authentic operational grounding.

```{python}

#| output: false

from pathlib import Path

def _p(name):
    p = Path(f"../data/processed/clusters/{name}")
    return p if p.exists() else Path(f"data/processed/clusters/{name}")

_words_gap = json.loads(_p("channel_gap_words_robustness.json").read_text())
promo_ratio = _words_gap["promo_per_1k_words"]["ratio"]
promo_call = _words_gap["promo_per_1k_words"]["call_mean"]
promo_filing = _words_gap["promo_per_1k_words"]["filing_mean"]
quant_ratio = _words_gap["quant_per_1k_words"]["ratio"]
quant_call = _words_gap["quant_per_1k_words"]["call_mean"]
quant_filing = _words_gap["quant_per_1k_words"]["filing_mean"]
```

Our cross-venue data directly reject this trade-off. When measuring narrative density per 1,000 words of disclosure across venues, earnings conference calls contain **`{python} f"{promo_ratio:.1f}"`× more promotional statements** than statutory filings (rising from `{python} f"{promo_filing:.3f}"` to `{python} f"{promo_call:.3f}"` claims per 1,000 words). Crucially, however, calls amplify observable quantification even more: conference calls contain **`{python} f"{quant_ratio:.1f}"`× more quantified outcome claims** than formal filings (rising from `{python} f"{quant_filing:.3f}"` to `{python} f"{quant_call:.3f}"` claims per 1,000 words, @fig-promotion-and-evidence).

This establishes an essential empirical insight: **promotion and evidence rise together rather than trade off across venues**. Because the relative amplification in quantified evidence exceeds that of promotional claims (`{python} f"{quant_ratio:.1f}"`$\times >$ `{python} f"{promo_ratio:.1f}"`$\times$), oral conference calls do not merely inflate hype—they serve as the primary venue where managers provide concrete operational metrics to the market. Conversely, formal SEC filings are unpromotional not because they possess superior operational grounding, but because their language gravitates toward generic, unanchored legal boilerplate. Rhetorical tone alone is therefore an inadequate proxy for corporate credibility.

## Regulatory Scrutiny as an External Stress Test

When regulatory scrutiny directly questions a firm's AI claims, does the issuer correct the specific deficiency, and does it alter its broader disclosure posture? We examine nine S&P 500 corporations receiving formal SEC comment letters regarding artificial intelligence between 2022 and 2025 — the most recent, Welltower, on 2025-04-28; a keyword re-scan of all SEC correspondence filed since then through 2026-05-27 finds no additional AI-related letter. Each treated issuer is evaluated against three trajectory-matched industry peers in a stacked cohort event study centered on the first Form 10-K filed post-scrutiny ($k = 0$), comparing overall AI disclosure intensity ($D$) against the specific operational dimension scrutinized by staff (matching procedures and the 9-firm inventory are detailed in Appendix F, @tbl-g1-sec-letters).

## What Credibility Means in This Thesis

Synthesizing evidence across escalating commitments yields three core takeaways: within-disclosure decoupling between narrative intensity and grounded substance is persistent ($\rho \approx 0.60$); cross-venue divergence reflects missing evidence in statutory filings rather than different operational activity mixes; and direct regulatory scrutiny induces targeted compliance without closing broader credibility gaps. AI washing in this thesis therefore denotes an observable, persistent decoupling between narrative intensity and verifiable operational substance—not legal proof of fraud or nonimplementation.

# Market Relevance of Disclosure Signals

Do investors see through this decoupling, or does the market reward rhetoric over substance?

This chapter investigates whether capital markets reflect the *volume* of corporate AI rhetoric or the *substance* of operational execution around earnings calls. Tracking communication call-by-call across S&P 500 firms from 2021 to 2025, we evaluate how post-call market beta correlates with established disclosure postures, call-specific narrative surprises, and concrete operational activities, conditioning on pre-call beta.

## Empirical Strategy and Research Design

The unit of observation is a firm-date earnings call event. Multiple transcripts occurring on the same day are aggregated, and calls with zero mentions are retained as valid empirical zeros. The call date anchors the timeline:

- **Historical Posture ($\text{HistD}_{i,t^{-}}, \text{HistS}_{i,t^{-}}$):** Expanding mean of disclosure intensity and substance across calls strictly prior to date $t$.
- **Call-Specific Surprise ($\text{SurpriseD}_{i,t}, \text{SurpriseS}_{i,t}$):** Current call value minus the firm's historical mean ($\text{Value}_{i,t} - \text{Hist}_{i,t^{-}}$).
- **Disclosure Intensity ($D$):** AI frames per 1,000 words.
- **Disclosed Substance ($S$):** $S = \log(1 + n_{\text{activities}}) \times G$, where activity grounding ($G$) is the proportion of activities meeting concrete verification criteria.

Pre- and post-call market betas are estimated over non-overlapping windows to avoid look-ahead bias and earnings-announcement drift:

- $\beta^{\text{pre}}_{i,t}$ over $[-252, -21]$ trading days before the call.
- $\beta^{\text{post}}_{i,t}$ over $[+21, +126]$ trading days after the call.

Predetermined controls ($X^{\text{pre}}_{i,t}$) include log market cap, 60-day return momentum ($\text{Return}_{60}$), and pre-call idiosyncratic volatility. Point-in-time accounting fundamentals (ROA, leverage) are linked from the most recent 10-K or 10-Q filed strictly before the call ($\text{filing\_date} < \text{call\_date}$), extracted from XBRL accession facts.

## Incremental Information of AI Decoupling

Before evaluating call-by-call return and beta dynamics, we test whether the firm-year AI-washing index ($W$) adds explanatory power beyond disclosure volume and substantive activity. Adding $W$ to the baseline beta specification raises $R^2$ from 0.1732 to 0.1735 ($n = 711; \Delta R^2 = +0.0004$; Wald $F = 0.12, p = 0.725$). 

While the credibility gap is persistent and managerially interpretable within Chapter 5's disclosure framework, it carries essentially zero incremental information about systematic equity risk once disclosure intensity and disclosed substance are already in the model.

## Baseline Econometric Model

We estimate an ANCOVA specification conditioning on pre-call beta:

$$
\beta^{\text{post}}_{i,t} = \alpha + \beta_1 \text{HistD}_{i,t^{-}} + \beta_2 \text{HistS}_{i,t^{-}} + \beta_3 \text{SurpriseD}_{i,t} + \beta_4 \text{SurpriseS}_{i,t} + \gamma \beta^{\text{pre}}_{i,t} + \delta X^{\text{pre}}_{i,t} + \alpha_{s,y} + \epsilon_{i,t},
$$

with industry-by-year fixed effects ($\alpha_{s,y} \equiv \text{SIC2} \times \text{Year}$) and standard errors clustered by firm. Continuous regressors are standardized to zero mean and unit variance.

@tbl-call-beta-baseline and @fig-call-beta-baseline report the baseline estimates.


```{python}

def _bp(var):
    row = base_ai.set_index("variable").loc[var]
    p_str = "< 0.001" if row["p"] < 0.001 else f"= {row['p']:.3f}"
    return row["beta_std"], row["p"], p_str

hd_b, hd_p, hd_pstr = _bp("hist_disclosure")
hs_b, hs_p, hs_pstr = _bp("hist_substance")
sd_b, sd_p, sd_pstr = _bp("surprise_disclosure")
ss_b, ss_p, ss_pstr = _bp("surprise_substance")

def _sig(p):
    return "positive and significant" if p < 0.05 else "not statistically significant"

_disc_joint = _formal["joint_disclosure_terms"]
_sub_joint = _formal["joint_substance_terms"]
_partial_r2 = _formal["partial_r2_ai_block"]
```

The baseline estimation covers `{python} f"{int(_baseline_sample['n_calls']):,}"` calls across `{python} int(_baseline_sample['n_firms'])` firms (`{python} int(_baseline_sample['n_fe_cells'])` industry-by-year cells, $R^2 =$ `{python} f"{_baseline_sample['r2']:.3f}"`). The median firm has `{python} f"{_baseline_sample['median_prior_calls']:.1f}"` prior calls in the panel, ensuring well-anchored historical averages.

Two main patterns emerge:

1. **Disclosure is `{python} _sig(sd_p)` at the call-specific margin:** Historical disclosure intensity is `{python} _sig(hd_p)` ($\beta =$ `{python} f"{hd_b:.3f}"`, $p$ `{python} hd_pstr`); call-specific surprise disclosure is $\beta =$ `{python} f"{sd_b:.3f}"` ($p$ `{python} sd_pstr`). Established rhetorical posture carries a robust association with subsequent systematic risk conditional on pre-call beta; a single call's disclosure surprise on its own does not.
2. **Substance does not:** Historical substance ($\beta =$ `{python} f"{hs_b:.3f}"`, $p$ `{python} hs_pstr`) and surprise substance ($\beta =$ `{python} f"{ss_b:.3f}"`, $p$ `{python} ss_pstr`) are indistinguishable from zero. Joint tests confirm this contrast: the disclosure block ($\text{HistD} + \text{SurpriseD}$) is significant ($F =$ `{python} f"{_disc_joint['F']:.2f}"`, $p =$ `{python} f"{_disc_joint['p']:.3f}"`; partial $R^2 =$ `{python} f"{_partial_r2:.4f}"`), whereas the substance block is null ($F =$ `{python} f"{_sub_joint['F']:.2f}"`, $p =$ `{python} f"{_sub_joint['p']:.3f}"`).

Executive disclosure volume, anchored in a firm's historical rhetorical posture, is associated with post-call market beta conditional on pre-call risk, while grounded operational activities show no incremental association.

## Robustness and Identification

@tbl-call-beta-paper evaluates the baseline ANCOVA model against specifications incorporating accounting controls, alternative estimation horizons, the Fama–French three-factor benchmark, firm fixed effects, and first-differencing.

```{python}
fe_df = fe.set_index("variable")
delta_df = delta.set_index("variable")
ff3_df = ff[ff["block"] == "ff3"].set_index("variable")

vars_map = [

rows = []
for v_key, v_label in vars_map:

rows.append(["Beta pre", "✓", "✓", "✓", "✓", "✓", "—"])
rows.append(["Market controls", "✓", "✓", "✓", "✓", "✓", "✓"])
rows.append(["Accounting (ROA, Lev)", "—", "✓", "—", "—", "—", "—"])
rows.append(["SIC2 × CallYear FE", "✓", "✓", "✓", "✓", "—", "✓"])
rows.append(["Firm FE", "—", "—", "—", "—", "✓", "—"])
_acct_n = int(samples.set_index("model").loc["beta_post_126_accounting_M1", "n_calls"])
rows.append(["N",
             f"{int(base_win.loc['hist_disclosure', 'n_calls']):,}" if "n_calls" in win.columns else "—",

headers = ["Variable", "Baseline", "+ Acct.", "FF3", "[+21,+252]", "Firm FE", "Delta Beta"]
Markdown(tabulate(rows, headers=headers))
```

The baseline result survives accounting controls (ROA and liabilities/assets), alternative post-call estimation horizons (up to a full trading year, $[+21, +252]$), and the Fama–French three-factor benchmark, but attenuates and disappears under within-firm (firm fixed effects) and first-difference ($\Delta\beta$) specifications. This identifies the association as predominantly cross-sectional sorting rather than a call-induced change in systematic risk: firms that talk heavily about AI systematically carry higher market risk than peers, but high-frequency quarterly shifts in disclosure do not exogenously alter firm risk. Full diagnostics, leverage specifications (Debt/Equity and Liabilities/Assets), and influence tests are reported in Appendix E.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
loyo = pd.read_csv(find_path("data/processed/clusters/call_beta_robustness_leave_one_year_out.csv"))
placebo = pd.read_csv(find_path("data/processed/clusters/call_beta_robustness_placebo.csv")).set_index("variable")

loyo_hd = loyo[loyo["variable"] == "hist_disclosure"].set_index("block")
_min_hd = loyo_hd.loc[loyo_hd["beta_std"].idxmin()]
_min_hd_year = _min_hd.name.replace("excl_", "")
_max_p_hd = loyo_hd["p"].max()
_all_hd_sig = bool((loyo_hd["p"] < 0.05).all())
_hd_sig_text = "significant across every excluded year" if _all_hd_sig else f"significant in every excluded year except {_min_hd_year}"
_hd_detail_text = "" if _all_hd_sig else f", where it drops to $\\beta = {_min_hd['beta_std']:.3f}$ (p = {_min_hd['p']:.3f})"

loyo_sd = loyo[loyo["variable"] == "surprise_disclosure"].set_index("block")
_any_sd_sig = bool((loyo_sd["p"] < 0.05).any())

pb_disc, pb_sub = placebo.loc["disclosure"], placebo.loc["substance"]
_pb_disc_p = "< 0.001" if pb_disc["p"] < 0.001 else f"= {pb_disc['p']:.3f}"
_pb_sub_p = "< 0.001" if pb_sub["p"] < 0.001 else f"= {pb_sub['p']:.3f}"
```

## Critical Limitations

1. **HistDisclosure is not concentrated in a single year, but SurpriseDisclosure never reaches significance on its own:** Leave-one-year-out regressions keep $\text{HistDisclosure}$ `{python} _hd_sig_text` ($p \le$ `{python} f"{_max_p_hd:.3f}"``{python} _hd_detail_text`). $\text{SurpriseDisclosure}$, by contrast, `{python} "reaches p < 0.05 in at least one excluded-year specification" if _any_sd_sig else "never reaches conventional significance in any single-year exclusion"`, consistent with its null result in the baseline specification: the association between call disclosures and post-call market beta runs through a firm's persistent historical disclosure posture, not through the surprise content of any one call.
2. **Pre-call beta placebo failure:** Regressing pre-call beta ($\beta^{\text{pre}}_{[-252, -21]}$) on contemporaneous call disclosure yields $\beta =$ `{python} f"{pb_disc['beta_std']:.3f}"` ($p$ `{python} _pb_disc_p`), while substance is null ($p$ `{python} _pb_sub_p`). Firms that talk heavily about AI were already high-beta firms prior to the call. $\text{HistDisclosure}$ therefore reflects a persistent corporate posture adopted by high-beta, growth-oriented firms seeking market attention, rather than an exogenous shock to systematic risk.

# From Measurement to Managerial Application

Chapters 2 through 6 developed, validated, and tested a multi-layer measurement pipeline across more than nine million paragraphs of corporate text. The framework translates the empirical architecture into five sequential diagnostic questions ($D \to A \to G \to S \to W$), complemented by within-firm cross-venue consistency. @tbl-managerial-framework summarizes their managerial and investment interpretation.

| Core Due-Diligence Question | Construct | Managerial & Investment Decision Read |
|---|---|---|
| **1. How much are they saying?** | Disclosure Intensity ($D$) | **Narrative Exposure:** Evaluates corporate attention to AI. High $D$ signals ambition or growth positioning, but absent grounding carries high rhetorical risk. |
| **2. What do they claim to be doing?** | Disclosed AI Activity ($A$) | **Claimed Scope:** Verifies whether the firm reports actionable initiatives across core business functions rather than relying on abstract buzzwords. |
| **3. How concrete is the disclosure?** | Grounding Quality ($G$) | **Evidentiary Rigor:** Assesses verification attributes (scaled deployment, named product/process, quantified metric, provider transparency). |
| **4. How much grounded substance is disclosed?** | Disclosed Substance ($S$) | **Effective Substantiation:** Evaluates total volume of grounded AI activity, rewarding operational depth while penalizing empty boilerplate. |
| **5. Is narrative running ahead of execution?** | Decoupling Index ($W$) | **Triage / Diligence Signal:** Flags firms whose narrative volume outstrips verified operational disclosure ($W \gg 0$) or quiet executors ($W \ll 0$). |
| **6. Does the story survive across venues?** | Cross-Venue Consistency | **Evidentiary Commitment:** Checks whether oral conference-call claims, metrics, and products are formally committed to statutory 10-Ks under legal liability. |

: The AI Disclosure Credibility Framework: translating measurement constructs into managerial decisions. {#tbl-managerial-framework}

: Illustrative peer comparisons across firm-years within Financials, Technology, and Real Estate. Evaluated for the focal FY2024 reporting cycle (with Welltower evaluated around its FY2024 Form 10-K filing and 2025 SEC comment letter). {#tbl-firm-comparisons}

**Microsoft (MSFT, FY2024):** Microsoft illustrates why aggressive communication need not imply decoupling: exceptional disclosure volume ($D = 1.350$, 100th percentile) is backed by the corpus's deepest AI activity inventory ($A = 137$ in FY2024) and substantial operational grounding ($S = 1.746$), producing commensurate substance with minimal ceremonial risk ($W = +0.014$).

**JPMorgan Chase (JPM, FY2024) vs. Goldman Sachs (GS, FY2024):** JPM and Goldman illustrate why similar disclosure intensity can conceal divergent operational profiles within the same industry. In FY2024, both report moderate disclosure intensity ($D \approx 0.048\text{--}0.049$). However, JPM anchors its communication in formal governance oversight ($G = 0.364$, 60% governance share) and internal workflow integration, whereas Goldman's AI disclosures remain concentrated in defensive legal risk factors ($60\%$ risk share, zero deployed AI activities disclosed, $G = 0.169$, $W = +0.210$).

**Apple (AAPL, FY2024):** Apple exemplifies the Governance-Led posture: corporate communication deliberately emphasizes proprietary on-device processing and consumer privacy safeguards rather than speculative commercialization claims, maintaining tight discipline between narrative volume and operational footprint ($D = 0.249$, 54% governance share).

**Welltower (WELL, FY2024 SEC Comment Letter):** Welltower provides direct empirical validation of the cross-venue credibility framework and illustrates how narrative divergence attracts regulatory intervention. In its Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2024, Welltower's AI disclosure was confined to a single generic statement on page 40 that the firm was "integrating generative AI tools into [its] systems" ($D = 0.047$, 73% risk share). However, on its fourth-quarter 2024 earnings call (February 15, 2025), executive leadership claimed an "industry-leading" proprietary data science platform and touted it as a primary competitive advantage. On April 28, 2025, the SEC Division of Corporation Finance issued a formal comment letter citing this exact cross-venue asymmetry, instructing management to explain the discrepancy and formally disclose the actual operational status of its data science platform in statutory filings [@welltower2025letter, p. 1].

## Portfolio-Scale Application: Screening the S&P 500

Connecting Chapter 3's communication archetypes with Chapter 4–5's operational diagnostics yields an actionable decision engine:
$$\boxed{\text{Clusters (Archetypes) = Describe current communication posture (Ch 3)}}$$
$$\boxed{A, G, S, W, \text{Venue Gap} = \text{Diagnose operational substance and evidentiary quality (Ch 4--5)}}$$
$$\boxed{\text{Portfolio Screens / Strategic Playbook} = \text{Act (Ch 7)}}$$

### The AI Disclosure Decision Heuristic for Due Diligence

Rather than mapping firms into static corporate classes, the framework organizes due-diligence decisions into a 2×2 decision heuristic defined by **Disclosure Intensity ($D$)** and **Disclosed Substance ($S$)** (@tbl-screening-matrix). Crucially, $W$ is not a fraud classifier ($W \neq \text{Legal Wrongdoing}$); rather, $D$ and $S$ determine the quadrant action, while $W$ prioritizes diligence depth within quadrants.

| | Low Disclosed Substance ($S$) | High Disclosed Substance ($S$) |
|---|---|---|
| **High Disclosure Intensity ($D$)** | **INVESTIGATE**<br>Audit specific claims, examine operational stage, metrics, products, and providers; compare oral calls against statutory filings. Highest priority for forensic due diligence ($W \gg 0$). | **VALIDATE**<br>Confirm that documented evidence is cross-venue consistent and that grounding is sustained over reporting periods ($W \approx 0$). |
| **Low Disclosure Intensity ($D$)** | **DEPRIORITIZE / MONITOR**<br>Low AI narrative exposure coupled with minimal reported AI activity; requires no intensive diligence unless corporate disclosure posture shifts ($W \approx 0$). | **EXPLORE**<br>Investigate potential "quiet substance": concrete, highly grounded operational AI activity deployed with minimal promotional fanfare ($W \ll 0$). |

: AI Disclosure Decision Heuristic: turning disclosure intensity and disclosed substance into due-diligence action. *Disclosure Intensity ($D$) and Disclosed Substance ($S$) are the empirical measures developed in Chapters 3–5; the heuristic organizes action priorities without introducing additional corporate typologies.* {#tbl-screening-matrix}

### Four Operational Portfolio Screens

Across disclosing S&P 500 firm-years, analysts execute four targeted screens:

- **Investigate:** Rank firm-years by high $W$ where narrative volume outstrips verifiable operational substance.
- **Validate:** Rank prominent high-substance firm-years by $S$ to confirm leaders anchored in deep operational execution.
- **Explore:** Identify strongly negative $W$ to uncover quiet operational capability under-communicated to financial markets.
- **Reconcile:** Rank cross-venue disconnects where executive call rhetoric outpaces signed statutory filings (exemplified by the SEC inquiry into Welltower).

@tbl-screening-screens applies these screens to the S&P 500 firm-year panel and reports representative priorities.

## Strategic Alignment for Corporate Issuers

For corporate executives (CFOs, Investor Relations teams, and Chief Strategy Officers), the framework evaluates whether external communication matches internal strategic reality:
$$\boxed{\text{Locate current archetype (Ch 3)} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{Assess substance } (S) \;\longrightarrow\; \text{Define actual AI strategy} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{Choose action}}$$

@tbl-issuer-matrix maps the firm's observed Chapter 3 archetype against the actual business-model role of AI (Core Technology, Material Operational Enabler, or Supporting/Peripheral).

| Observed Posture (Ch 3 Archetype) | Strategic Role of AI | Operational Diagnosis ($S, W$) | Recommended Strategic Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Vocal Substantive** | AI-Core | High $S$, $W \approx 0$ | **SUSTAIN & ALIGN:** Maintain evidentiary density, report milestone updates, and ensure identical substance across conference calls and statutory filings. |
| **Vocal Substantive** | Supporting / Peripheral | Low $S$, $W \gg 0$ | **RETREAT:** Over-communicating; curb promotional rhetoric and ungrounded narrative claims to avoid market skepticism and regulatory inquiry. |
| **Defensive Discloser** | Supporting / Peripheral | Low $S$, $W \approx 0$ | **STAY SELECTIVE:** Completely rational and appropriate; disclose only what is strictly material to financial reporting and risk factors. |
| **Defensive / Governance-Led** | Material Enabler / Core | High $S$, $W \ll 0$ | **COMMUNICATE EVIDENCE:** Sub-communicating capability; surface existing operational deployments and quantified productivity without inflating promotional hype. |

: Strategic AI Disclosure Alignment Matrix: operational guidance for corporate issuers and disclosure committees. {#tbl-issuer-matrix}

To implement this alignment, corporate disclosure committees execute a five-step sequence:

1. **Locate Observed Archetype:** Benchmark current corporate communications against Chapter 3's empirical profiles (*Vocal Substantive*, *Governance-Led*, *Defensive*).
2. **Assess Disclosed Substance:** Measure AI activity volume ($A$), operational grounding ($G$), and decoupling index ($W$) against industry peers.
3. **Define Actual Strategic Role:** Establish internally whether AI is core, an operational enabler, or a peripheral vendor tool.
4. **Choose Target Action:** Select the appropriate strategic response: *Sustain & Align*, *Retreat*, *Stay Selective*, or *Communicate Evidence*.
5. **Enforce Cross-Venue Consistency:** Audit draft conference call remarks against signed Form 10-K disclosures to prevent promotional or evidentiary divergence.

## Managerial Takeaways and Operational Checklist

Issuers use the framework to align communication with actual strategic importance. Investors use it to prioritize diligence rather than mechanically rank firms. Regulators and boards can use the same signals for triage, not as evidence of wrongdoing. @tbl-checklist summarizes the resulting decision rules for both issuers composing corporate communications and investors evaluating them.

| Dimension | Issuer Implementation Guidance | Investor / Analyst Due Diligence Read |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Named AI Activity** | State the specific action-object pair (e.g., "automated underwriting algorithm"), not generic placeholders like "AI capabilities." | Absence of a discrete action-object pair is the single most common disclosure gap (observed in 86% of disclosing firms). Treat unanchored claims as ceremonial rhetoric. |
| **2. Operational Stage** | Explicitly distinguish between exploratory pilots and deployed/scaled production systems. | Heavily discount "piloting" or "exploring" statements. Only scaled and deployed implementations correlate with distinct financial fundamentals. |
| **3. Named Product or Process** | Identify the proprietary brand, commercial tool, or internal workflow by name. | Named claims provide falsifiable verification points and carry substantial incremental explanatory power in fundamental asset pricing models. |
| **4. Quantified Outcome** | Disclose measured operational impacts (cost reduction %, revenue share, latency improvements) in statutory filings, not just calls. | Verify whether oral conference-call metrics appear in signed SEC filings. In the corpus, quantified outcome disclosure drops from 61% pooled to 37% in filings. |
| **5. AI Provenance & Partner** | Disclose whether the AI solution is proprietary, third-party licensed, or co-developed with commercial vendors. | 16% of AI activities in the corpus leave technology origin unstated; unstated provenance heavily clusters in the least-grounded defensive segment (33%). |
| **6. Venue Consistency** | Maintain evidentiary coherence between oral earnings call discussions and signed statutory 10-Ks. | Cross-venue divergence can attract regulatory scrutiny when claims made in voluntary communications are insufficiently reflected or substantiated in filings. |

: The AI Disclosure Credibility Checklist: operational guidance for corporate issuers and investment due diligence. {#tbl-checklist}

# Conclusions

This thesis follows a single progression: AI disclosure became nearly universal; its content differs systematically across firms; those differences reveal meaningful gaps between talk and disclosed substance, especially across disclosure venues; and finally, we ask whether these distinctions carry economic information—finding that some do, although the evidence is associative rather than causal.

First, as AI disclosure reached near-universal adoption across the S&P 500, firms organized into reproducible disclosure profiles. However, only Vocal Substantives—those reporting the greatest concrete AI activity even after conditioning on volume—exhibit a broad, sector-year-adjusted economic distinction on corporate fundamentals.

Second, credibility is institutionally contingent. The within-disclosure washing index captures a stable firm-year gap between disclosure intensity and grounded substance, while cross-venue comparisons reveal that the same firm-year places 9.9× more promotional claims and 17.1× more quantified claims in earnings calls than in statutory filings. Direct SEC comment-letter scrutiny was followed by suggestive letter-aligned adjustments, but no detectable broader change in claim specificity or decoupling.

Third, semantic content and disclosed AI activity relate to economic and market outcomes, but the evidence is associative rather than causal. In earnings-call beta regressions, historical disclosure posture predicts higher post-call systematic risk, but this reflects a persistent trait of high-beta firms rather than an exogenous communication shock. Once underlying disclosure intensity and disclosed substance are observed, the washing index adds no incremental explanatory power.

The methodological contribution is a five-layer, largely reproducible extraction pipeline that recovers structured, falsifiable claims and grounded AI activities from over nine million paragraphs at a cost no purely human-coded design could match, with venue-specific measurement error documented rather than assumed away. The managerial contribution is a concrete disclosure checklist for issuers and a cross-venue credibility framework for investors, both grounded in what the measurement shows carries information.

Theoretically, the results are most consistent with a signalling account of specificity, a legitimacy/institutional-diffusion account of the "no AI" segment's disappearance, and a cheap-talk account of earnings calls as a more discretionary, lower-formality disclosure venue. The main claims of this thesis are measurement and association rather than causal effects: the most tightly identified design isolates a venue-associated disclosure difference, not the causal effect of legal liability.

Four limitations are carried through every chapter:

1. Operational extraction relies on zero-shot LLM inference: while audited against a 720-text human ground-truth sample (89.1%–95.8% field agreement) and cross-model agreement benchmarks ($\kappa = 0.81–0.87$), residual algorithmic noise remains possible in complex borderline disclosures.
2. "Disclosed AI activity" measures what a firm says it does, not what an audited operational record would confirm.
3. Direct SEC comment letters on AI are rare in the S&P 500 ($N=9$), limiting statistical precision; point estimates indicate directionally higher narrative volume and suggestive letter-aligned adjustments, but aggregate specificity and washing indices show flat null responses with wide uncertainty.
4. The AI-washing index has no external benchmark: it compares a firm's own disclosure to its own disclosed AI activity, both extracted from the same corpus, and cannot check either against an audited operational record.

Cross-venue results are robust to using words rather than paragraphs as the denominator and to denominator-free AI activity comparisons.

Future research should extend the cross-venue design to a synthetic-control or matched-donor-pool setting if a denser call-transcript series becomes available, particularly for cases like Welltower with too little pre-period call content to estimate a firm-specific trajectory; and extend the comparative international panels (Chile, Italy) noted in the data section to test whether the venue-gap and segmentation results generalize outside a single, SEC-regulated regime.

# Appendices {.unnumbered}

## Appendix A: Data, Computational Environment and Pipeline {.unnumbered}

### Computational infrastructure and analytical stack {.unnumbered}

The data processing pipeline and empirical analysis were implemented in Python 3.11. Data storage follows a parquet-first architecture where DuckDB provides queryable virtual views over physical parquet partitions without duplicating disk storage. `pandas` and `NumPy` handle panel construction, financial alignments, and matrix operations; `scikit-learn`, `SciPy`, and `statsmodels` execute prefilter training, dimensionality diagnostics, cluster modeling, and cluster-robust econometric regressions; and `matplotlib` generates all analytical figures.

Text representations employ the Hugging Face dense embedding model `BAAI/bge-m3` (1,024-dimensional dense vectors) for semantic-anchor scoring and cosine-similarity retrieval. The production inference judge is `qwen/qwen3.7-flash`, queried via OpenRouter with schema-constrained JSON outputs enforced through `pydantic-ai` for both semantic-frame classification and disclosed-activity extraction. Gemini is reserved strictly as an independent cross-validation judge for inter-annotator agreement benchmarks, rather than as a primary extraction engine.

High-throughput embedding generation and LLM prompt batches were executed on a dedicated GPU instance (Vast.ai) equipped with an NVIDIA RTX 5090 running a containerized data-science runtime image. Econometric estimation, panel joins, and document compilation were performed locally on Apple Silicon (M2 Pro, 32 GB RAM). Code artifacts are version-controlled with Git and data assets synchronized via Backblaze B2. SEC statutory filings (10-K, 10-Q, DEF 14A, 8-K, 20-F) and XBRL disclosures were harvested via EDGAR tooling adhering strictly to SEC fair-access rate limits (10 req/s). Earnings call transcripts were acquired and processed through dedicated financial audio/text parsers. Market price series and the daily Ken French Fama–French three-factor series provide the daily risk-free and market excess returns for asset-pricing specifications.

### Multi-stage data processing pipeline {.unnumbered}

The data processing pipeline operates across five sequential stages:
1. **Document acquisition and segmentation:** Statutory filings and earnings call transcripts are retrieved, cleaned, and segmented into semantic paragraphs and conversational speaker turns.
2. **Text deduplication and filtering:** Scorable paragraphs (retaining text with $>3$ characters and alphanumeric tokens) are hashed using BLAKE2b to remove boilerplate disclaimers and cross-filing duplicates.
3. **AI-relevance prefiltering:** A 39-signal Gradient Boosted Decision Tree (GBDT) prefilter ($\tau = 0.17$) scores scorable texts to identify candidate paragraphs containing substantive artificial intelligence content while filtering out background noise.
4. **Semantic frame extraction:** Candidate paragraphs are evaluated by the production LLM judge (`qwen/qwen3.7-flash`), which classifies them into multi-dimensional managerial posture frames (promotional, risk, governance, temporal, positioning, and specificity).
5. **Concrete AI activity extraction:** A second-pass structured prompt extracts discrete, firm-conducted corporate AI activities, identifying action types, maturity stages, target audiences, proprietary vs. third-party sourcing, and specific named entities.

### GBDT AI-relevance prefilter feature weights and signal importance {.unnumbered}

To identify candidate paragraphs containing genuine corporate discussion of artificial intelligence across nearly ten million raw passages without incurring prohibitive inference costs or injecting keyword-matching bias, the pipeline deploys a 39-signal Gradient Boosted Decision Tree (`HistGradientBoostingClassifier`, depth 4, decision threshold $\tau = 0.17$).

The model addresses three key failure modes of traditional dictionary lookups and linear logistic classifiers:

1. **Context dilution:** In statutory filings (particularly DEF 14A proxy statements and 8-K voting reports), AI keywords frequently occur as isolated cells within massive board skill matrices or incidental biographical summaries (e.g., *"director serves on the advisory board of Scale AI"*). Linear keyword matching assigns equal weight to these passages, whereas tree-based interactions penalize long texts with low term density.
2. **Document-channel neutrality:** Statutory document form (10-K, 10-Q, DEF 14A, 8-K, Call) is *deliberately excluded* from the feature set. Including filing form would cause the model to memorize channel-specific baseline frequencies rather than textual signals, inducing circularity into subsequent cross-venue comparisons.
3. **Asymmetric loss function:** Because prefilter false negatives represent permanent sample attrition that cannot be recovered downstream, while false positives merely incur a fraction of a cent in LLM validation cost, the decision threshold was calibrated on holdout samples with an asymmetric loss preference ($\beta = 2.0$, prioritizing recall over precision).

To quantify how the trained model discriminates relevant corporate statements, @tbl-a0-gbdt-feature-importance reports the permutation feature importance ($\Delta \text{Average Precision}$, 10 random shuffles with sample weights) across the three underlying signal tiers:

- **Sentence-level AI embeddings (67.4% total weight):** The fraction of sentences containing an AI keyword (`ai_sent_share`, 46.5% relative weight) and the raw count of AI-bearing sentences (`sent_n_ai`, 14.9%) overwhelmingly dominate the classification. Rather than evaluating paragraph-level dense embeddings where AI mentions are diluted by unrelated text, isolating and scoring only the specific sentences that mention AI provides the cleanest discriminative signal.
- **Text structure and formatting disqualifiers (21.5% total weight):** Character length (`log_len`, 13.0%) and numeric digit frequency (`digit_rate`, 2.8%) serve as strong structural filters that penalize dense tabular disclosures, financial schedules, and multi-page governance matrices. Conversely, the density of first-person corporate pronouns (`first_person_per_100w`, 2.1%) acts as an affirmative marker of managerial voice (*"we deployed"*, *"our platform"*).
- **Paragraph semantic anchors and lexical matches (11.1% total weight):** Dense cosine similarities against category anchors contribute localized contextual signal, led by strong lexical terms (`strong_ge1`, 3.8%), risk posture (`score_ai_risk`, 1.6%), and outcome realization (`score_ai_outcome`, 1.3%).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-a0-gbdt-feature-importance
#| tbl-cap: "Permutation feature importance and signal decomposition for the 39-signal GBDT AI-relevance prefilter model."
#| echo: false
import json
from pathlib import Path
from tabulate import tabulate
from IPython.display import Markdown

def _p(name):
    p = Path(f"../data/processed/clusters/{name}")
    return p if p.exists() else Path(f"data/processed/clusters/{name}")

data = json.loads(_p("gbdt_prefilter_importance.json").read_text())
features = data["features"][:16]

rows = []
for f in features:
    imp_str = f"{f['importance_mean']:.4f} ± {f['importance_std']:.4f}"
    pct_str = f"{f['rel_importance_pct']:.1f}%"
    rows.append([f["tier"], f"`{f['feature']}`", f["description"], imp_str, pct_str])

headers = ["Signal Tier", "Feature Name", "Description / Linguistic Function", "Permutation ΔAP", "Relative Weight"]
Markdown(tabulate(rows, headers=headers))
```

*Notes:* Permutation feature importance computed across 10 random permutations on the combined golden benchmark and cross-channel tuning sample ($n = 12,269$ annotated paragraphs, scoring metric: Average Precision). Top 16 features shown (accounting for 96.2% of total feature importance); the complete 39-feature dictionary is archived in the project's processed-data store.

## Appendix B: Measurement and Validation {.unnumbered}

### Validation protocol and inter-annotator agreement {.unnumbered}

To verify construct validity and quantify measurement error across the pipeline, we conducted double-annotation validation protocols across both prefilter selection and semantic extraction stages:

1. **Prefilter precision and recall:** A stratified random sample of 300 paragraphs evaluated across the GBDT decision boundary ($\tau = 0.17$) confirmed an empirical precision of 91.2% and recall of 88.7% against full-text human review.
2. **Semantic frame reliability:** A multi-judge evaluation set comprising 300 frame-labeled paragraphs (434 distinct frame annotations) yielded high inter-rater reliability between independent judges (Cohen's $\kappa \in [0.81, 0.87]$ across frame categories), establishing that promotional, governance, and risk orientations represent statistically distinct and stable linguistic constructs.
3. **Disclosed AI activity grounding:** An audit of 120 activity-bearing paragraphs containing 267 extracted discrete corporate actions was validated using the specialized `ui-validator` annotation tool. Field-level agreement reached 92.4% on business function identification, 89.1% on operational stage classification, and 95.8% on entity role assignment (distinguishing internal proprietary brands from external commercial vendors).

### Error taxonomy and classification robustness {.unnumbered}

Systematic error analysis reveals that extraction discrepancies are heavily concentrated at the margin between forward-looking promotional claims and early-stage exploratory research descriptions. Importantly, these borderline cases exhibit zero systematic correlation with firm size, leverage, or sector classification. Collapsing or adjusting the weighting of borderline categories leaves the resulting firm-level posture scores and archetype assignments virtually identical (Spearman $\rho > 0.96$ across all specifications), demonstrating that downstream empirical findings are robust to residual measurement noise.

```{python}
SEGS = ["Vocal Substantives", "Governance-Led Disclosers", "Defensive Disclosers", "No AI"]

g = df.groupby("archetype")
n = df["archetype"].value_counts()

unspecified_source = [f"{100 - df[(df.archetype==s)&has_activity]['share_proprietary_ai'].mean()*100 - df[(df.archetype==s)&has_activity]['share_third_party_ai'].mean()*100:.1f}%" for s in SEGS]

    ["Firms reporting quantified outcome metrics (%)"] + pct_any("any_quantified_outcome"),
```
